args.body:
MEMORANDUM

TO: Engagement File
FROM: White Collar Defense & Investigations Group
RE: Negotiation Analysis — Government Counter-Markup of Deferred Prosecution Agreement (Financial Services Company)
DATE: [Engagement working date]
MATTER FILE 26 — WHITE COLLAR DEFENSE INVESTIGATIONS

PRIVILEGED & CONFIDENTIAL — ATTORNEY WORK PRODUCT
PREPARED IN ANTICIPATION OF LITIGATION / NEGOTIATION

------------------------------------------------------------------------
I. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
------------------------------------------------------------------------

We have reviewed the government's counter-markup to the Deferred Prosecution Agreement ("DPA") for our client, a financial services company, against (a) the original DPA as initially circulated and (b) our firm's initial markup proposing firm-standard and market-standard positions. The government's counter-markup accepts most of the firm-standard provisions but introduces three material deviations that must be reconciled against the base materials and the controlling partner instruction:

   1. Indemnification cap silently reduced, and the basket converted from a deductible to a tipping basket;
   2. The definition of Material Adverse Effect ("MAE") amended to add carve-outs for regulatory action of exactly the kind at issue in this matter; and
   3. A new limitation period that shortens the survival period for the core representations.

Pursuant to the controlling partner instruction set out in the deal-team correspondence (the latest message in the thread, which supersedes all earlier messages), our negotiating posture is:

   • BASKET CONVERSION: The client will CONCEDE the basket conversion (deductible to tipping basket). This is no longer a contested point.
   • SURVIVAL-PERIOD REDUCTION: Any reduction in the survival period for the core representations is a WALK-AWAY ISSUE. We must reject the government's new limitation period and preserve the survival matrix set forth in Exhibit B.

The MAE carve-out deviation is not squarely resolved by the partner instruction and therefore requires careful substantive analysis and a recommended counter-position, taking into account Schedule 3.7 and Schedule 5.2.

------------------------------------------------------------------------
II. SCOPE OF THE COMPARISON AND GOVERNING RECORD
------------------------------------------------------------------------

The operative record for this analysis comprises (i) the original DPA as circulated, (ii) our firm's initial markup, (iii) the government's counter-markup, (iv) the disclosure schedules and exhibits, and (v) the deal-team correspondence containing the controlling partner instruction. Where any disclosure schedule or exhibit conflicts with a general statement in the base materials, the scheduled exception controls.

The DPA governs the resolution of the government's investigation into the client's conduct. Consistent with the U.S. Department of Justice's Principles of Federal Prosecution of Business Organizations (Justice Manual § 9-28.000 et seq.), a DPA is a negotiated resolution that reflects a compromise of the parties' respective positions. The analysis below identifies each deviation introduced by the government's counter-markup, evaluates it against the original DPA, our initial markup, and firm/market practice, reconciles it with the applicable schedules and exhibits, and recommends a negotiating position consistent with the controlling partner instruction.

------------------------------------------------------------------------
III. DEVIATION 1 — INDEMNIFICATION CAP AND BASKET MECHANICS
------------------------------------------------------------------------

A. Original DPA / Our Initial Markup Position

The original DPA and our initial markup contemplated an indemnification regime in which:
   • An indemnification cap set a clear, negotiated ceiling on the aggregate liability of the indemnifying party.
   • The compensating risk threshold operated as a DEDUCTIBLE basket — i.e., the indemnifying party bore the first dollars of loss up to the basket threshold, and claims were recoverable only to the extent they exceeded the basket.
   • A dedicated schedule (see Schedule 5.2) catalogued retained liabilities that the indemnification provisions were designed to leave in place and not silently shift.

B. Government's Counter-Markup

The government's counter-markup:
   • silently REDUCES the indemnification cap below the negotiated level; and
   • CONVERTS the basket from a deductible to a TIPPING basket — meaning that once the claim threshold is reached, the indemnifying party becomes liable for the full amount of all losses from the first dollar, not merely the excess over the threshold.

C. Reconciliation with Schedules and Exhibits

Schedule 5.2 lists retained liabilities that the markup's indemnification changes would SILENTLY SHIFT to the client. Because Schedule 5.2's retained-liability carve-outs control over general statements in the base materials, the government's adjustment to the cap and basket mechanics has direct, adverse consequences for those retained liabilities. Any concession on basket mechanics must be scoped so that Schedule 5.2 retained liabilities remain excluded from the indemnification regime, or the value of the concession is materially enlarged.

D. Recommendation and Negotiating Position

Consistent with the controlling partner instruction, the client will CONCEDE the basket conversion from a deductible to a tipping basket. We should therefore:
   • Accept the tipping-basket construct as a settled point and not re-argue it.
   • Negotiate to preserve as much of the indemnification cap as possible and, at minimum, hold the cap at the original negotiated level. While the basket mechanics are conceded, the cap reduction is a separate adjustment and should be challenged independently.
   • Confirm expressly in the final DPA that Schedule 5.2 retained liabilities are not swept into the indemnification regime by virtue of the basket conversion or cap change. The scheduled exceptions control, and we must ensure the drafting reflects that control rather than being undermined by the cap/basket edits.

------------------------------------------------------------------------
IV. DEVIATION 2 — MATERIAL ADVERSE EFFECT CARVE-OUTS FOR REGULATORY ACTION
------------------------------------------------------------------------

A. Original DPA / Our Initial Markup Position

The MAE definition in the original DPA and our initial markup reflected firm-standard drafting: a general adverse-effect standard subject only to enumerated, customary carve-outs. Critically, the definition did NOT include a carve-out for regulatory action of the kind at issue in this engagement.

B. Government's Counter-Markup

The government's counter-markup amends the MAE definition to add carve-outs for regulatory action "of exactly the kind at issue in this matter." In substance, the amendment would exclude the specific regulatory exposures central to this investigation from the MAE standard, shielding the government (and the agreement) from a finding of material adverse effect based on those regulatory events.

C. Reconciliation with Schedules and Exhibits

• Schedule 3.7 discloses TWO pending regulatory inquiries that intersect the markup's MAE carve-outs. The carve-outs proposed in the counter-markup are not general or hypothetical; they track the very matters enumerated in Schedule 3.7.
• Because the scheduled exceptions control over general statements in the base materials, Schedule 3.7's disclosure of these pending inquiries means the carve-outs, if accepted as drafted, would operate directly against our client's known exposure. The carve-out and the disclosed inquiry are functionally coordinated: the markup both (i) discloses the pending inquiries and (ii) excludes those same inquiries from the operation of the MAE clause.
• Schedule 5.2 is also relevant to the extent retained liabilities arising from the pending regulatory inquiries would otherwise be excluded from indemnification.

D. Recommendation and Negotiating Position

The MAE carve-out deviation is not addressed by the controlling partner instruction and therefore requires our firm recommendation, consistent with firm precedent and market practice:

   • REJECT the MAE carve-outs for regulatory action of the kind at issue in this matter. Carve-outs drafted to track the specific, disclosed regulatory inquiries (Schedule 3.7) would effectively neutralize the MAE protection as to the client's principal known exposure and are inconsistent with our initial markup and standard DPA practice, under which general regulatory or governmental-actions carve-outs are narrowly drawn and do not retroactively eviscerate disclosed exposures.
   • If the government insists on some regulatory-action carve-out language, we should COUNTER with a version that: (i) uses standard, generalized regulatory-action carve-out language; (ii) expressly de-scopes the carve-out so that it does not apply to the two pending regulatory inquiries identified in Schedule 3.7; and (iii) preserves the client's ability to invoke the MAE clause in the event of a material adverse effect stemming from any heightened or extended regulatory exposure arising from the subject conduct.
   • Reconcile the final MAE clause with Schedule 3.7 so that the clause does not silently undermine the section of the DPA that governs the pending inquiries.

------------------------------------------------------------------------
V. DEVIATION 3 — NEW LIMITATION PERIOD / SHORTENED SURVIVAL FOR CORE REPRESENTATIONS
------------------------------------------------------------------------

A. Original DPA / Our Initial Markup Position

The original DPA and our initial markup established the survival of the core representations in accordance with the survival matrix set forth in Exhibit B. That matrix defined the windows during which the core representations remain actionable, consistent with firm and market precedent for DPA negotiations.

B. Government's Counter-Markup

The government's counter-markup introduces a NEW limitation period that SHORTENS the survival of the core representations relative to the Exhibit B survival matrix.

C. Reconciliation with Schedules and Exhibits

Exhibit B sets the survival matrix that the markup's limitation-period change directly CONTRADICTS. Since the scheduled exhibits and their terms control over general statements in the base materials, the Exhibit B survival matrix represents the established baseline. The government's new limitation period is inconsistent with Exhibit B and, if accepted, would truncate the client's rights to assert claims relating to the core representations.

D. Recommendation and Negotiating Position

Consistent with the controlling partner instruction, any survival-period reduction is a WALK-AWAY ISSUE for the client. Our posture must therefore be:

   • REJECT in full the government's new limitation period insofar as it shortens the survival of the core representations.
   • INSIST that the survival of the core representations remain as set forth in Exhibit B, without reduction.
   • This is a hard, non-negotiable position: if the government does not withdraw the shortened survival period (or otherwise fails to preserve the Exhibit B survival matrix for the core representations), the matter should be treated as a walk-away. We should communicate this clearly and early so as to anchor the negotiation and avoid the government treating the survival concession as available.
   • No trade against this point should be offered; the survival-period reduction is not concedable under the controlling instruction.

------------------------------------------------------------------------
VI. RECOMMENDED NEGOTIATING POSTURE AND PRIORITIES
------------------------------------------------------------------------

The following reflects the controlling partner instruction (superseding any earlier conflicting priority ordering in the deal-team correspondence):

   PRIORITY 1 — SURVIVAL PERIOD (WALK-AWAY): The shortened limitation period for the core representations must be rejected outright. Preserve the Exhibit B survival matrix. This is the client's bright-line, walk-away point.

   PRIORITY 2 — MAE CARVE-OUTS (REJECT / COUNTER): Reject the MAE carve-outs for the regulatory action at issue. Counter with standardized regulatory-action carve-out language that de-scopes the two pending regulatory inquiries in Schedule 3.7 and preserves MAE protection for the client's known exposure. Reconcile the final MAE clause with Schedule 3.7.

   PRIORITY 3 — INDEMNIFICATION CAP (CHALLENGE INDEPENDENTLY): While the basket conversion is CONCEDED, the silent reduction of the indemnification cap should be challenged independently and held at the original negotiated level, consistent with the Schedule 5.2 retained-liability carve-outs remaining intact.

   CONCESSION — BASKET CONVERSION: The client will concede the conversion of the basket from a deductible to a tipping basket. We accept this point and should not re-litigate it; our focus is on ensuring the cap and the Schedule 5.2 retained-liability carve-outs are preserved notwithstanding the concession.

------------------------------------------------------------------------
VII. RISKS AND OPEN ITEMS
------------------------------------------------------------------------

   1. Scope of the basket concession. We must confirm in final drafting that the conceded tipping-basket mechanism does not claw Schedule 5.2 retained liabilities into the indemnification regime, which the counterparty's silent cap/basket edits would otherwise accomplish.
   2. Interplay of MAE carve-outs and Schedule 3.7. The MAE carve-outs, as drafted, are coordinated with the Schedule 3.7 disclosures. Any version of the MAE clause must be cross-checked against Schedule 3.7 to avoid evisceration of the client's known-exposure protections.
   3. Survival matrix integrity. Exhibit B is the controlling baseline for survival. The government's new limitation period must be withdrawn; we should track its status as the key deal-closing condition and treat failure to preserve Exhibit B as a walk-away event.
   4. Negotiation sequencing. Because the survival-period point is a walk-away issue, we recommend raising it first to anchor the negotiation and signaling that it is non-negotiable, then moving to the MAE carve-out counter, and finally negotiating the cap independent of the conceded basket.

------------------------------------------------------------------------
VIII. CONCLUSION
------------------------------------------------------------------------

The government's counter-markup introduces three deviations from the original DPA and our initial markup. Two of them — the basket conversion and the cap reduction — sit within the indemnification framework, with only the basket conversion being concedable under the controlling partner instruction. The MAE carve-out deviation, which is coordinated with the Schedule 3.7 disclosures and would neutralize the client's primary known-exposure protection, must be rejected and countered.
